output.headline: Senators push for stronger enforcement of Russia sanctions law
output.bodyHtml:
Democratic and Republican lawmakers challenged Donald Trump on Friday over a stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel, struck with Vladimir Putin, Russia’s president, as its four-and-a-half year war against Ukraine continued. The deal upended years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end the war and put Washington on a fresh collision course with Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and European allies.

Democrats said the agreement undercut a law Trump signed last month that allowed for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, and directed him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia, though the law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.

“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” the Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, joined by Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the Foreign Relations Committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Banking Committee, said in a statement. “Failure to follow the law and the bipartisan will of Congress that only weeks ago passed legislation aimed at cutting off revenue for Russia’s war machine and curbing purchases of Russian oil and gas.”

Some Republicans also criticised the agreement.

“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican, wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”

Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, calling it “absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.

Trump’s envoys, Steve Witkoff and his son-in-law Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war, as Trump announced the oil deal.

Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.

“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.

Perhaps the fiercest response came from Zelenskyy, who told Axios that it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 earlier this week.

In a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump, said the deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.

“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.

Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, in a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’s Nato allies, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war with Iran.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” Trump wrote.

“Based on the condition of their diesel refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 tons of diesel fuel.”

He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”

Fuel prices have risen sharply because of Iran’s closure of the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that carried 20 per cent of global oil supplies before the war. A gallon of fuel now averages $4.20, but it is the soaring price of diesel – which rose last month to a record high of $6.52 – that has caused the most political damage to Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterms approach.

Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need to operate machinery.

Zelenskyy rejected a recent request from Trump, who had criticised Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries and called on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets, saying Ukraine would stop only if Russia accepted a reciprocal de-escalation plan that halted Moscow’s attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.

The agreement also comes on the heels of rising tensions between Russia and Washington’s Nato allies in Europe, amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.

The latest development is likely to lead to a further deterioration of Zelenskyy’s relationship with the Trump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”

But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment in his failure to reach a deal.

Trump’s willingness to reach an agreement with Putin that will lower fuel costs comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of American forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.
output.standfirst:
Senators and some Republicans challenge Trump's deal with Vladimir Putin to buy Russian diesel, which Volodymyr Zelenskyy calls “absolutely terrible” and critics say undercuts US sanctions, straining relations with Ukraine and Nato allies

output.progress: Senators Schumer, Shaheen and Warren are challenging the deal by invoking a sanctions law passed last month to curb Russian oil revenue.

output.headline: Progressive voters return to Labour, party claims after byelection win
output.bodyHtml:
Labour’s deputy leader has claimed the party is winning back voters on the left who became disillusioned under Keir Starmer’s leadership, after it saw off Zack Polanski and the Greens to win the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.

Labour’s Sagal Abdi-Wali took 45% of a relatively low turnout to keep Starmer’s old north London seat for the party, pushing Polanski, who had stood for the party he leads, into second place on 33%.

Labour strategists were buoyed by the party’s relatively straightforward route to victory in a diverse inner-city area of the sort the Greens have been targeting with recent success, even though the result was broadly as predicted.

The result “sends a clear message to those voters who lost faith in Labour in recent years”, said Lucy Powell, who called last month for the party to unite progressive voters under Andy Burnham if it wants to win the next election.

After the byelection win, she told the Guardian: “We hear you, we’ve listened and we know we needed to be clearer about what we stand for and what type of country we want to see, proudly putting our values centre stage. We’re delighted so many of you are backing us once again.”

Ahead of the byelection, the Green party had voted at their conference last weekend to adopt a hugely controversial policy equating Zionism with racism, and saying Israel should be replaced with a single Palestinian state.

Polanski has faced criticism for showing minimal leadership on the most toxic internal debate the Greens have faced in living memory, with the chair of Jewish Greens saying he should resign.

The byelection, called after Starmer resigned his Commons seat shortly after he was ousted by Burnham, saw a turnout of 38.7%, possibly low in part because Labour’s win was so widely predicted, despite a major campaigning effort from the Greens.

The turnout also suggests Burnham could still face a battle to engage some voters in urban areas, particularly London, where the Greens took control of three councils in May’s local elections.

In an emotional victory speech, Abdi-Wali, a former child refugee who came to the UK from Somalia in the 1990s, hit out at “those who seek to divide us”, in what appeared to be a response to Reform UK’s Zia Yusuf, who suggested she was not British shortly after the byelection was called.

“I hope this moment says something about who gets to belong,” she said. “For people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here. This is Camden, and this is Britain.”

Polanski, who leads the Greens in England and Wales, responded by saying the result showed his party remained a major threat to Labour, with many voters telling him they wanted to “give Andy Burnham a chance”.

It was the Greens’ second best-ever byelection result, more evidence of the party’s increased prominence and campaigning power since Polanski became leader 13 months ago.

The Greens’ best byelection result came in February, when they took an equally safe Labour seat, Gorton and Denton in Greater Manchester, in a major upset that weakened Starmer’s position. Around the same time, the Greens peaked at 21% in national polling, above Labour. They are now about 11%, more than 15 points behind Burnham’s party.

Polanski’s position has come under scrutiny since the Zionism motion was passed, with critics accusing him of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate to campaign in the byelection, giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it.

Polanski said, in interviews after the byelection loss, that he would have voted against the motion had he attended, given that two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down.

On Friday, Vivien Lichtenstein, chair of Jewish Greens, said Polanski, who is Jewish, made a “big mistake” by avoiding the vote. Asked if he should continue in his role, she told Times Radio: “No, I think he should resign.”

However, other members of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.

Speaking shortly before the byelection result was announced, Caroline Lucas, the Greens’ former leader and first MP, said Polanski “should have been there and he should have voted”.

Speaking to Newsnight, she said: “I would have hoped that he would have really been a very strong critic of this motion, because the motion was flawed from top to bottom in my view. It’s dangerous, it’s divisive, it tries to have a singular definition of Zionism when we know that there are many.”

Asked if Polanski should stand down, Lucas did not definitively say he should remain as leader: “I think let’s just see what happens in the … coming days and weeks.”

There is no formal mechanism for ejecting a leader of the Greens. However, they are re-elected every two years, meaning Polanski, who took over in September 2025, will have to go before party members again in less than a year.
output.standfirst: Sagal Abdi-Wali’s win for Labour in Holborn and St Pancras put the party 15 points ahead of the Greens, who had been ahead in the polls before Keir Starmer resigned as prime minister.
output.progress: Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, says the party has listened to disillusioned voters and will be clearer about its values.

context.text: The victory reassures Andy Burnham in his first big electoral test as prime minister and reinforces polling showing he has recovered some public support Labour lost under Starmer.

output.headline: Standards inquiry into Farage's £5m gift nears its conclusion
output.bodyHtml:
Rival parties are readying themselves to contest a byelection in Clacton in the months ahead, as speculation grows that the standards inquiry into Nigel Farage’s £5m gift is nearing a conclusion.

Conservative sources said the party was ready to fight for Farage’s seat, though senior shadow cabinet figures are divided on whether it would be winnable, given Farage’s victory in a byelection over the summer.

Other parties, including the hard-right Restore Britain, are also expected to put up candidates in the seat this time, having boycotted the August poll.

Westminster is braced for a battle over the future of Reform should the sanction from the standards inquiry prove a heavy one.

The byelection could in theory take place before Christmas if a decision is imminent, though the timelines of previous cases suggest next year is more likely, should a serious sanction be imposed.

In the cases of Margaret Ferrier, the SNP MP who broke lockdown rules, and Peter Bone, the Tory MP found to have bullied staff, well over six months passed between the conclusion of the commissioner’s report and a byelection taking place.

The investigation into Farage’s gift began after the Guardian revealed in May that the crypto-billionaire Christopher Harborne had given him £5m just before the last election in 2024.

Farage has said the gift was a personal matter, not political, and that the money did not need to be declared, though the rules state that financial support related to an MP’s job must be registered if given in the 12 months before they enter parliament.

Under the process, if a serious breach is found, the commissioner will pass a memorandum to the standards committee of MPs and lay members.

They would then hold further discussions, call a hearing or invite evidence from the MP before deciding on a penalty, a process that can take weeks; the MP also has a right of appeal to the independent expert panel, which can take a further month or more.

Should parliament agree to a penalty of more than 10 days’ suspension from the House of Commons, voters in the constituency could then hold a recall petition, which needs signatures from 10% of them over a period of six weeks.

Conservatives are hopeful that Farage could decide not to fight, noting that in the cases of Bone and Ferrier, neither contested their seats. “There’s a question of whether he will stand again,” said one shadow cabinet minister.

But Reform sources insisted Farage would fight for his seat again, having won the summer byelection against independent candidates, including Count Binface, by more than 11,000 votes.

He has also embarked on a tour of the country to shore up his core support, alongside a reorganisation of his party HQ that includes launching a new Reform TV channel to carry the party’s message direct to voters, with a team of 12 “journalists” headed by the former GB News producer Aaron Lobo, who had been director of operations.

Farage won a majority of 8,000 at the last general election, beating the sitting Tory MP, Giles Watling, who had previously held the seat with a majority of more than 25,000 in 2019, when there was no Brexit party candidate standing.
output.standfirst: Rival parties, including the Conservatives and Restore Britain, are readying themselves to contest a Clacton byelection, as the standards inquiry into Nigel Farage’s £5m gift is rumoured to be nearing its end.

output.headline: Chris Bryant bans Drumcree march on safety grounds to prevent violence
output.bodyHtml:
The Northern Ireland secretary of state has banned the Drumcree parade, acting to head off violence after a 13-day impasse between the Orange Order and nationalists.

Chris Bryant announced on Friday night that it was “not in the public interest” for Orangemen to march the contested route through Garvaghy Road in Portadown, which Catholic residents had blocked.

He said he acted on advice from Jon Boutcher, the chief constable of the Northern Ireland Police Service, that the parade “would carry an unacceptable risk of serious injury, disorder and a wider contagion effect” across Northern Ireland.

The Parades Commission ruled two weeks ago that a small, circumscribed march could pass along Garvaghy Road – a reversal of 28 years of successive bans. But police held the Orangemen back after thousands of residents and supporters, including Sinn Féin leaders, blocked the road.

Garvaghy Road residents welcomed the secretary of state’s decision, saying it brought relief and certainty after a tense standoff that revived memories of the 1990s, when Orangemen fought pitched battles with police trying to march the route.

It was the only “sensible, reasonable and logical outcome”, said Breandán Mac Cionnaith, of the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition.

The Sinn Féin leader, Mary Lou McDonald, and the party’s Northern Ireland first minister, Michelle O’Neill, said in a statement that residents had endured fear and anxiety. “There will be an enormous sense of relief within the community this evening.”

The Irish government welcomed the decision and appealed to both sides to seek common ground. “This isn’t a time for triumphalism or claiming victories or anything like that,” said the taoiseach, Micheál Martin. “Those on the unionist, loyalist side will look at this through a different prism. We need to be conscious of that. We need to acknowledge that.”

Gavin Robinson, the Democratic Unionist party (DUP) leader, accused Boutcher and Bryant of bowing to republican agitation and threats of potential violence. “These decisions are a mistake, and send profound signals that the country should be run on force of numbers and who shouts the loudest. The framework for both parading and protests now lies in tatters, and the rule of law has been fundamentally undermined.”

Robinson called on the secretary of state to explain what the government would do to “restore confidence in the rule of law”.

Related: Artists including Noel Gallagher show support for Garvaghy Road residents in Drumcree dispute

Earlier on Friday the chief constable asked Bryant to review the Parade Commission’s determination, made last month, that conditions in Portadown enabled the parade to go ahead.

“I’ve looked at the changing situation in Portadown, the fact that it’s very difficult for that procession to proceed, and I’ve decided that it’s not in the public interest for it to proceed, and I’ve therefore banned the procession,” said Bryant.

He thanked Portadown’s Orange Lodge for its “peaceful and law-abiding approach” and regretted that both sides could not reach a compromise, leading to a standoff. “With this in mind, I call for all protests, rallies and demonstrations to be stood down. There is no excuse for a continued ratcheting up of tensions.”

Boutcher said the dispute had affected relationships within and between communities and the police. “It is in everyone’s interest that time and space is now created for conversations about finding long-term solutions to this complex and sensitive issue.”

The dispute has fuelled angry exchanges at the Stormont assembly and destabilised the executive, with unionists demanding O’Neill step down as first minister for allegedly breaking the law at a Garvaghy Road protest.

O’Neill said she would cooperate with the investigation after the PSNI, earlier on Friday, sent the Sinn Féin deputy leader a letter probing alleged criminal offences relating to her involvement in the protest.
output.standfirst: Chris Bryant’s decisive ban on the Drumcree parade is meant to head off an assessed risk of renewed violence, bringing relief to Garvaghy Road after a 13-day standoff between the Orange Order and nationalists that divided Stormont.
output.progress: Chris Bryant has called for all protests to stand down, and the police chief says conversations on long-term solutions can now begin.

output.headline: World leaders and clergy call for a more humane path on executions
output.bodyHtml:
Worldwide condemnation has met a “barbaric” plan to execute a disabled man by firing squad and livestream it to the public, with critics comparing the Trump administration to dictatorships in Iran and Afghanistan.

The Pentagon confirmed on Thursday that the execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at a military base at Fort Hood in Texas in 2009, would be livestreamed on 3 December.

The United Nations’ office of the high commissioner for human rights warned on Friday that broadcasting the killing would amount to a public execution and “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.

Related: Pentagon says execution of Fort Hood shooter will be livestreamed

Politicians, religious leaders and human rights advocates in the US and abroad voiced opprobrium at the plan. Hillary Clinton, the former US secretary of state, wrote on social media: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.”

Yassamin Ansari, the first Iranian American Democrat elected to the US Congress, posted: “In Trump’s America, we’re doing public executions now. WTF. This is what happens under brutal dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan. It’s all part of Trump’s authoritarian takeover of the United States.”

Britain moved to distance itself from the execution, having abolished the death penalty in the 1960s. Bridget Phillipson, the UK’s equalities minister and Labour party chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that she found the concept “rather disturbing”.

Phillipson stressed that the decision was a matter for the US government, adding: “They are a close ally. Does that mean that we support everything the US government does? No.”

Under US military law, a president must approve an execution by firing squad; Trump approved Hasan’s on the recommendation of his defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, the Pentagon said.

JD Vance – a practicing Catholic – told reporters on Friday he wouldn’t watch the livestreamed execution of Hasan, but stopped short of criticizing the administration’s decision.

When asked how his Christian beliefs influence his view of the public execution, Vance dismissed controversy about the manner of execution and appeared to question whether the livestream will happen.

“Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope the people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” the US vice-president told reporters. “That said, if it’s ultimately livestreamed, I’m not going to be watching it.”

Hegseth confirmed the livestream plan after previously saying that the execution would be public. Speaking to the conservative broadcaster Real America’s Voice, he said people should be able to watch because they need to understand that there were “serious consequences” for such crimes.

Asked whether Hasan had made any final requests, Hegseth replied: “Don’t care. We’ll see him on December 3.”

Now 56, Hasan was sentenced to death by a military jury in 2013 after being convicted of 13 counts of premeditated murder and 32 counts of attempted premeditated murder. Twelve of those killed and 30 of the wounded were soldiers.

The former army psychiatrist opened fire with a handgun at a medical facility at Fort Hood on 5 November 2009 as soldiers waited for medical checks before deployment. He was shot by a police officer during his arrest and left partly paralysed, and now uses a wheelchair.

The execution is expected to be the first by firing squad carried out by the US military since 1945, when army private Eddie Slovik was executed for desertion during the second world war. The last US military execution of any kind took place in 1961, when John Bennett was hanged.

Hasan’s case comes amid renewed scrutiny of capital punishment in the US following the botched lethal injection of Tennessee death-row prisoner Christa Pike last week. Her lawyers said she awoke in hospital “angry and confused” and remained seriously ill and shackled to her hospital bed.

Courts have in the past blocked media attempts to televise US executions, and no other country is known to televise or livestream legal executions, experts said.

Indeed, public executions have largely disappeared around the world. Amnesty International recorded at least 17 in 2025, including 11 in Iran and six in Taliban-run Afghanistan.

In the US, executions have been conducted privately for about nine decades. The hanging of Rainey Bethea in Kentucky in 1936, witnessed by thousands, is generally regarded as the country’s last public execution, although another hanging took place in Missouri the following year.

Experts said there was no known precedent for livestreaming a legal execution. The execution of the Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001 was made available to victims’ relatives through closed-circuit television, but was not broadcast publicly.

Religious leaders also criticised the plan. Archbishop Paul Coakley, president of the US Conference of Catholic Bishops, said it was a “barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered”.

Politicians from both sides of the aisle also spoke out against the plan. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House of Representatives armed services committee, said it was “disturbing and makes a mockery of our legal system”. The Democratic senator Chris Murphy described public executions as “medieval”.

The Republican senator Thom Tillis said Hasan should face the death penalty but that broadcasting his execution was “beyond disgusting”, arguing that public executions were associated with oppressive regimes.

Others warned that the spectacle would be counterproductive and act as a recruiting sergeant for US enemies seeking fresh propaganda.

Ned Price, a former deputy to the US representative to the United Nations, posted on X: “You can take it from those of us who’ve spent years working on terrorism: the surest way to spawn more radicalized zealots is to glorify violence, embrace a cult of death, and create a martyr for the cause.

“Or take it from [al-Qaida] and ISIS, whose tactics offer the closest modern-day approximation of Hegseth’s proposal. Either way, it’s hard to conjure a more vivid example of his trademark performative bravado, which routinely damages America’s image and, in this case, so ghoulishly leaves us more vulnerable.”

Legal experts have raised the possibility that the live stream could be challenged in court. Eugene Fidell, a military law specialist at Yale Law School, said Hasan could seek legal action to block the public display of his death.

Elisabeth Semel, co-director of the Death Penalty Clinic at the University of California, Berkeley, said the announcement raised serious questions about the dignity of the condemned prisoner and the government’s motivation for staging such an unusual spectacle.

“This is a president who’s about spectacle and that’s, I think, precisely the message that he intends to deliver,” she told the Associated Press.

Justin Mazzola, deputy director of research at Amnesty International USA, said: “Livestreaming the taking of a life by firing squad would only compound the cruelty of the death penalty and perpetuate the cycle of violence that the authorities purportedly seek to end.

“This announcement adds to the display of cruelty that we have just witnessed in the senseless pursuit of the execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee. The US death penalty is irredeemably broken. It is high time that the US authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all.”

Other experts argued that public access could increase transparency around capital punishment. Deborah Denno, a death penalty specialist at Fordham University, told the AP that a live stream could make the process more transparent at a time when the botched execution in Tennessee had renewed questions about how the state puts prisoners to death.

It remains unclear whether Hasan will seek to challenge his execution in civilian court, a move that could significantly delay the proceedings.
output.standfirst:
World leaders, politicians and clergy are calling for a more humane approach after the Pentagon confirmed its plan to livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, convicted of killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.

  • US politics live – latest updates
output.progress: Politicians across party lines, religious leaders, the UN and rights groups have condemned the plan, and legal experts say Hasan could challenge it in court.

output.headline: Crown estate sets out plans for profitable new future at Royal Lodge
output.bodyHtml:
The lease on Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor’s former Royal Lodge home in Windsor has been officially surrendered, after the ex-prince faced a £1.8m bill to cover repair and restoration of the property.

The crown estate spokesperson said: “The lease for Royal Lodge has ended and our focus now is firmly on its future use and the opportunities to generate additional financial value for the nation from its early return.”

The property will now be marketed by two nationally recognised agents, the crown estate spokesperson added, as attention turns to its future use.

Andrew was granted £302,000 in compensation for giving up the lease on the 98-acre property early, bringing his total costs for leaving to £1.5m.

Recouping costs for dilapidations is a standard process when a lease ends, and the Guardian understands the repairs covered the entire estate, which includes several properties, gardens and large outbuildings.

Andrew was entitled to the compensation because, as per the terms of his lease, he surrendered it within the first 25 years.

King Charles has reportedly contributed to the repair costs, the Times reported.

The former Duke of York moved out of the Windsor mansion this year as the US Department of Justice released files related to the child sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

He was forced to move to Marsh Farm on the king’s Sandringham estate in Norfolk, amid public outcry over the rent he had paid on the Royal Lodge.

In June, a National Audit Office investigation established that the late queen’s second son had received an undisclosed amount of private income from subletting three cottages on the Royal Lodge estate, while paying a peppercorn rent – a small, symbolic payment – for more than two decades.

On Thursday, Mountbatten-Windsor won a legal challenge against Thames Valley police over search warrants used to raid his home. The former prince brought a judicial review of the legality of the force’s actions and those of the central criminal court, which granted the warrants.

Mr Justice Hilliard, sitting at the high court in central London, said Thames Valley police (TVP) had conceded that it obtained the search powers under the wrong statutory provision and ruled that the warrants were unlawful.

Police believe the ruling will not affect the success of the investigation, though the episode is embarrassing for TVP.

The arrest followed information that emerged from the Epstein files. It was alleged that when Mountbatten-Windsor was the UK’s trade envoy he shared sensitive information with Epstein. Police began searching the former duke’s residence on the Sandringham estate and the Royal Lodge on the same day as his arrest. Documentary material and electronic devices were seized.

Late last year, King Charles stripped his brother of his right to be a prince and of his dukedom over his association with Epstein.

Mountbatten-Windsor receives an annual stipend, the amount of which has not been disclosed, from King Charles’s private funds, but a palace source told reporters it had been made clear this should not be used to fund the judicial review.
output.standfirst: The crown estate plans a profitable new future for Royal Lodge after the lease ended, following a £1.8m repair bill partly offset by £302,000 in compensation to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor.
output.progress: The crown estate is marketing Royal Lodge through two agents to generate financial value for the nation from its return.

output.headline: Vast majority of Lib Dem MPs back Ed Davey, deputy leader says
output.bodyHtml:
Daisy Cooper, the Liberal Democrats’ deputy leader, immediately backed Ed Davey, saying he enjoyed the support of the ‘vast majority of MPs’, who wanted him to lead them into the next election and were ‘furious at this distraction’.

‘We Liberal Democrats are the last line of defence against a Reform UK government, and Ed is determined to lead a strong and united party into the next general election whenever it comes,’ Cooper said.

‘As Ed said at conference, we are in the fight of our lives against the right who want to turn our country into their version of Trump’s America.’

Her defence of Davey came as he faced a growing revolt against his leadership of the Liberal Democrats, following the resignation of a senior frontbench figure on Friday.

Charlie Maynard, the Liberal Democrat Treasury spokesperson, resigned in an attempt to unseat Davey after months of frustration over concerns that the party is failing to cut through with voters, the Guardian understands.

Maynard’s resignation, first reported by the Financial Times, came four days after Alison Bennett, the Lib Dem care and carers spokesperson, stood down from the frontbench.

Davey has led the party since 2019, first as acting leader and then officially from August 2020. At the 2024 general election, he steered the party to its most successful result in more than 100 years. The party now has 71 MPs, and is the third largest party in the House of Commons.

But the Lib Dems have slipped to fourth or fifth in national opinion polls, behind the Greens and Reform UK, and frustration has mounted over the party’s failure to attract voters in a fragmented political landscape.

At the party’s conference in Brighton in September, Davey played down criticism from a Liberal Democrat council leader who questioned whether he was the right person to lead the party. Julian Brazil, the leader of Devon county council, said the party was ‘sleepwalking into irrelevance’ and ‘lacking ambition’.

Davey announced a plan for a £17bn income tax cut in a speech aimed at shoring up the party’s support among former Conservative voters. He said the cut would be paid for entirely by increased growth generated by rejoining the EU’s single market and customs union.

However, Davey faced opposition from Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference to change the pension triple lock to help fund a national care service. One said his defence of the current policy ‘gaslights an entire generation into believing it’s for our benefit’.
output.standfirst: Davey has the backing of the ‘vast majority’ of Lib Dem MPs, his deputy says, after Treasury spokesperson Charlie Maynard resigned in a bid to unseat him as the party slips in the polls.
output.progress: Cooper points to Davey's record as grounds for confidence, including the party's best general election result in more than 100 years and its 71 MPs.

output.headline: Florida mobilises National Guard and shelters to aid Isaias response
output.bodyHtml:
The governors of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida declared states of emergency ahead of Hurricane Isaias, urging residents of some coastal communities to evacuate and many more to prepare for what was likely to be the storm's violent arrival.

Florida's national guard deployed roughly 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, the AP reported, as some prisons evacuated their incarcerated populations and most flights were grounded at several airports in Florida's Panhandle.

The state guard also deployed about 400 soldiers to assess the hurricane's damage and assist with route clearance, among other duties.

The Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission readied 10 airboats, 18 shallow-draft boats, nine ATVs and six larger platform vessels in case of damage or flooding.

Uber also partnered with the state to offer free round trips, worth up to $40 each way, to and from state-approved evacuation shelters.

Alabama governor Kay Ivey announced, shortly before the hurricane made landfall, that Donald Trump had approved the emergency declaration for her state. 'This will help cut tape for our federal partners to aid in any response,' Ivey said.

Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, Florida, on Friday evening, sweeping ashore from the northern Gulf of Mexico as the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season.

The National Hurricane Center (NHC) in Miami said the centre of the cyclone made landfall at 9.30pm ET as a category 2 hurricane with winds reaching 105 mph (165km/h). Two hours later, it was downgraded to a category 1 storm.

'Isaias makes landfall near Destin, Florida,' the NHC's latest update said. 'Life threatening storm surge affecting Gulf coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash flooding spread inland.'

Forecasters had expected Isaias to weaken from its peak earlier on Friday as a major category 3 hurricane because of shifts in wind speed.

But even as a weaker storm system, the NHC warned of a life-threatening storm surge affecting the Gulf coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash floods spread inland. The hurricane is expected to cross Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on the weekend, the agency added.

Warnings included a storm surge of up to 7ft (2.1 metres) along the Alabama-Florida line, and powerful wind gusts reaching parts of northern Georgia.

In the Florida Panhandle, Isaias's early impacts also came into view. In Panama City Beach, Noaa officials observed a water level 5.4 feet (1.64 metres) above average. About 125 miles west, at Pensacola city hall, a wind gust of up to 102 mph (164km/h) was recorded.

In Pensacola, about 50 miles (80km) west of Destin, an Agence France-Presse reporter witnessed howling winds rip the roofs from some homes and businesses, snapping tree branches as the power went out.

'Things are flying really fast, and I've never seen wind this fast before, so it's intense, it's scary,' Jonathan Ramos, a 40-year-old government employee, said from his hotel in Pensacola, where the power went out.

'I don't recommend people coming down here for fun to do this.'

Powerful gusts of wind and heavy rainfall appeared to down the canopy of a Crestview gas station on Friday evening, according to a video captured by meteorologist Nick Stewart. The tattered cover hung on top of the filling station.

'The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads,' Florida governor Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard "throughout the region".

The Mobile office of the National Weather Service warned parts of Florida could see 'extremely dangerous' tornado-like winds.

By Friday evening, nearly 500,000 customers had lost power across Alabama and Florida, according to PowerOutage.com.

'Things are going to get really, really treacherous,' Jamie Rhome, deputy director for the National Hurricane Center, told the AP.

Isaias is notable as one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.

Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15 per cent of crude pumped annually in the US.

In a sign of how seriously the warnings were being taken, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company's website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and is often a measuring stick of a storm's severity.

Kelsei Frazier, a Florida native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.

'We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it's not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed,' said Frazier. 'Which is a pretty big deal.'

Associated Press contributed reporting.

output.headline: Existing laws and surfer knowledge offer a way to save prized waves
output.bodyHtml:
Researchers say some of the world’s greatest surf breaks can be protected from the climate crisis, even as rising sea levels submerge some and coastal developments crush others.

An analysis of dozens of famous waves in world surfing reserves (WSR) found more than three-quarters at high risk from changing tide levels, hardened shorelines and shifting sands.

The changes matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.

The waves identified as most at risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde beach in north Devon, UK, the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador, and the Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.

The best surfing waves form through intricate combinations of sea-floor shape, swell direction and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena – a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen – and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a co-author of the study.

Researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves, even as global heating pushes up sea level and changes rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement in ways that can upset the delicate balance and destroy a wave.

Trent Hodges, a co-author of the study and a senior programmes manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR programme in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coalmine too – when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”

Almost 200 local experts analysed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar risk.

A key finding was that more natural coastlines could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments, while development such as sea walls, jetties and groynes made beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.

Adam Hall, a co-founder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”

He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants and car parks when the swells are good in January, February and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

The researchers want more local surfers to use the tools they have developed to assess their own breaks, and to work with local authorities and other groups to protect waves from coastal development and climate change.

Some places already protect their waves this way: the city of Gold Coast in Australia has put surf protection into planning law; New Zealand designates surf breaks of “national significance”; and Peru’s Ley de rompientes (law of the breakers) protects listed surf breaks.”

“Surfing is a huge driver of local economies,” Hodges said. “So whether you’re a surfer or not, that money supports local businesses, hotels, lodgings and so on.”

In Santa Cruz, surfing brings in about $200m (£151m) a year, he said.

“In the east of El Salvador, you have some of the most perfect point break waves you will find, and the entire economy there is pretty much dependent on surfing,” Hodges added.
